'''Sheila Rowan''' (born 25 November 1969) is a Scottish physicist and academic, who is Professor of Physics and Astronomy at the [[University of Glasgow]] in Scotland, and director of its [[Institute for Gravitational Research]] since 2009.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gla.ac.uk/schools/physics/staff/sheilarowan/|title=University of Glasgow - Schools - School of Physics & Astronomy - Our staff - Prof Sheila Rowan|website=gla.ac.uk|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.physics.gla.ac.uk/igr/index.php?L1=members&L2=member&name=srowan|title=University of Glasgow :: Schools :: School of Physics and Astronomy :: Research :: Research Groups - Institute for Gravitational Research - Our Staff and Students - Personal details|website=physics.gla.ac.uk|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="gla.ac.uk">{{cite web|url=https://www.gla.ac.uk/news/archiveofnews/2016/june/headline_462955_en.html|title=University of Glasgow - University news - Archive of news - 2016 - June - Professor Sheila Rowan appointed Chief Scientific Adviser|website=gla.ac.uk|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref> She is known for her work in advancing the detection of gravitational waves. In 2016, Rowan was appointed the (part-time) [[Chief Scientific Advisor]] to the [[Scottish Government]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Sheila Rowan, University of Glasgow|url=http://www.aps.org/about/governance/election/rowan.cfm|access-date=2020-08-19|website=aps.org|language=en}}</ref> She is a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]], the [[Institute of Physics]], and the [[Royal Society]]. She has been awarded the [[Philip Leverhulme Prize]] for Astronomy and Astrophysics, and the [[Fred Hoyle Medal and Prize]]. She was appointed MBE in 2011 and promoted to CBE in 2021.

==Education==
Rowan was born on 25 November 1969 in [[Dumfries]], Dumfriesshire, Scotland.<ref name="WW 21">{{cite web |title=Rowan, Prof. Sheila, (born 25 Nov. 1969), Professor of Experimental Physics, since 2006, and Director, Institute for Gravitational Research, since 2009, University of Glasgow; Chief Scientific Adviser to Scottish Government (part-time secondment), since 2016; President, Institute of Physics, from Oct. 2021 |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U291018 |website=[[Who's Who 2021]] |publisher=Oxford University Press |access-date=11 April 2021 |language=en |date=1 December 2020}}</ref> She was educated at [[Maxwelltown High School]], a [[comprehensive school]] in Dumfries.<ref name="WW 21" /> She studied physics at the [[University of Glasgow]], graduating with a [[Bachelor of Science]] (BSc) degree in 1991 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (PhD) degree in 1995.<ref name=rphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Glasgow|url=http://theses.gla.ac.uk/3422/|title=Aspects of lasers for the illumination of interferometric gravitational wave detectors|first= Sheila|last=Rowan|date=1995|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.294173}}|website=theses.gla.ac.uk|oclc=181873685}}</ref> Her PhD was research on [[gravitational wave]]s and was supervised by [[James Hough]].<ref name="gla.ac.uk"/>

==Career==
After her PhD, Rowan's work was split between the University of Glasgow and the [[Edward Ginzton]] Laboratory at [[Stanford University]].<ref name="gla.ac.uk"/> Since 2003, she has been based solely in Glasgow, and in 2006 was appointed Professor of Experimental Physics. Rowan's research has focused on developing optical materials for use in gravitational wave detectors.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Professor Sheila Rowan MBE|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/people/sheila-rowan|access-date=2020-08-19|website=GOV.UK|language=en}}</ref> She led a team which worked on the international Laser [[Interferometry|Interferometer]] [[Gravitational wave|Gravitational-Wave]] Observatory ([[LIGO]]) collaboration. This collaboration led in September 2015 to the detection of gravitational waves for the first time after [[Albert Einstein]]'s prediction.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Professor Sheila Rowan FRAS FRS MBE elected a Fellow of the Royal Society|url=https://ras.ac.uk/news-and-press/news/professor-sheila-rowan-fras-frs-mbe-elected-fellow-royal-society|access-date=2020-08-19|website=The Royal Astronomical Society|language=en}}</ref>

In June 2016, Rowan was seconded (part-time) to chief scientific advisor to the [[Scottish Government]],<ref name=frs/> a position vacant since December 2014, when [[Muffy Calder]] stood down.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-scotland-politics-36478219|title=New chief scientific adviser appointed|date=8 June 2016|access-date=8 December 2017|website=bbc.co.uk|author=Anon|publisher=[[BBC News]]}}</ref><ref name="gov.scot"/> In June 2021 she stepped down from this role and became the President of the [[Institute of Physics]], taking up her post on 1 October 2021.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.iop.org/about/news/new-iop-council-members-take-up-posts | title=New IOP Council members take up posts }}</ref> She was succeeded by [[Julie FitzPatrick]] who took up the post of [[Government Chief Scientific Adviser (United Kingdom)|Scotland's Chief Scientific Adviser]] on 14 June 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scottish Government appoint Julie Fitzpatrick as new chief scientific adviser |url=https://www.thenational.scot/news/19350219.scottish-government-appoint-julie-fitzpatrick-new-chief-scientific-adviser/ |access-date=2022-06-24 |website=The National |date=4 June 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==

* Rowan was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh]] (FRSE) in 2008<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.rse.org.uk/fellow/sheila-rowan/|title=Professor Sheila Rowan MBE FRSE - The Royal Society of Edinburgh|work=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|access-date=2017-12-18|language=en-GB}}</ref> and a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2018/05/distinguished-scientists-elected-fellows-royal-society-2018/|title=Distinguished scientists elected as Fellows and Foreign Members of the Royal Society |publisher=The Royal Society|date=9 May 2018|access-date=10 May 2018 }}</ref><ref name="frs">{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/sheila-rowan-13839/|title=Sheila Rowan|website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>
* Rowan was awarded the [[Philip Leverhulme Prize]] for Astronomy and Astrophysics in 2005, elected a [[Fellow of the Institute of Physics]] (FInstP) in 2006 and awarded [[Fellow]]ship of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2012.<ref name="frs" /> She was awarded the [[Fred Hoyle Medal and Prize]] of the [[Institute of Physics]] in 2016 in recognition of her pioneering research on aspects of the technology of gravitational wave observatories.
* In 2016, Rowan and her team contributed to the 2016 Special [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]], for their work on the first detection of gravitational waves, which was announced in February 2016.<ref name="gov.scot">{{cite web|url=https://beta.gov.scot/about/how-government-is-run/directorates/advanced-learning-and-science/sheila-rowan/|title=Professor Sheila Rowan MBE - gov.scot|website=beta.gov.scot|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref>
* In 2016, Rowan was among a team of researches to be awarded the President's Medal by the Royal Society of Edinburgh.<ref>{{Cite web|title=President's Medals for gravitational wave researchers|url=https://www.gla.ac.uk/myglasgow/news/archives/2016/november/headline_498051_en.html|access-date=2020-08-19|website=gla.ac.uk|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0" />
* In 2017, Rowan won the [[Suffrage Science award]]<ref name=suff>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gla.ac.uk/news/archiveofnews/2017/march/headline_517116_en.html|title=Suffrage Science awards for UofG physicists|website=www.gla.ac.uk}}</ref>
* In July 2019, Rowan was elected to the role of president-elect by the [[Institute of Physics]]. She took up the post of President on 1 October 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://beta.iop.org/iop-new-president-elect-and-council-members-2019|title=Institute of Physics announces new president-elect and Council members|website=Institute of Physics announces new president-elect and Council members {{!}} Institute of Physics|language=en|access-date=2019-07-31}}</ref>
*In 2020, Rowan won the [[Harold Hartley (chemist)|Sir Harold Hartley]] Medal by the [[Institute of Measurement and Control]] for outstanding contribution to the technology of measurement and control.<ref>{{cite journal |title=InstMC 2020 Awards |journal=Precision |date=December 2020 |volume=18 |page=20 |url=https://www.instmc.org/Portals/0/Publications/Precision%20Magazine/InstMC%20PRECISION%20Magazine_Issue%20No.18_December%202020.pdf?ver=2020-11-18-101637-387}}</ref>
* Rowan was appointed [[Member of the Order of the British Empire]] (MBE) in the [[2011 Birthday Honours]],<ref name="gla.ac.uk" /> and promoted to [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) in the [[2021 New Year Honours]] for services to science.<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=63218|supp=y|page=N9|date=31 December 2020}}</ref>

== Patents ==

* Rowan was awarded a patent for [[silicon carbide]] bonding in 2010 by the [[European Patent Office]]. The patent covers a novel method for bonding silicon carbide components to themselves and to other materials.<ref>{{Cite patent|title=Silicon carbide bonding|pubdate=2010-02-10|country=EP|number=1737802|assign=[[University of Glasgow]]|inventor1-last=Rowan|inventor1-first=Sheila|inventor2-last=Hough|inventor2-first=James|inventor3-last=Elliffe|inventor3-first=Eoin John}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Silicon Carbide Bonding|url=https://www.gla.ac.uk/connect/businessandinnovation/licensing/easyaccessipdeals/headline_179965_en.html|access-date=2020-08-19|website=gla.ac.uk|language=en}}</ref>
